newsitem.title: USA: Leading S.C. newspaper endorses Thurmond opponent.
newsitem.headline: Leading S.C. newspaper endorses Thurmond opponent.

text.p: One of South Carolina's largest newspapers on Sunday endorsed Republican Sen. Strom Thurmond's opponent, while the state's other leading paper offered a critical and tepid endorsement of the 93-year-old lawmaker.
The Greenville News endorsed Democratic political newcomer Elliott Close over Thurmond, saying "It is uncertain ... Sen. Thurmond can perform important duties during his work day."

The State newspaper of Columbia, South Carolina's capital, said of Thurmond, "South Carolinians love him, and he has demonstrated his love for our state for longer than most of us have been alive. But running for office at age 93 is no way to show that affection. He should have retired to make way for a more viable conservative."
Thurmond, running for his eighth term in the U.S. Senate, is chairman of the Armed Services Committee. His mental ability at the helm of the important military affairs committee has been questioned.

A Mason-Dixon poll released a week ago found Thurmond favoured by 50 percent of respondents compared to Close at 40 percent, with 10 percent undecided. A recent CBS poll found 60 percent of South Carolina voters seriously troubled by Thurmond's age.

The State said that by "ego and his refusal to deal with the inevitable limitations of ageing," Thurmond had put voters in the position of choosing between an icon whose mental agility is diminished and a Democratic sacrificial lamb whose credentials are too weak to make him a credible alternative.
The State predicted Thurmond would be re-elected because "polite people won't sit him down against his will."

The Greenville News said it would prefer to endorse Thurmond for his "exceptional constituent service" and "predictable conservative votes," but worried whether he could give "focused attention to extended discussion."
The paper also found Close, 43, qualified for the job, calling him a "man of intellectual honesty and high purpose."
In advertisements and in speeches across the state, Close, heir to the Springs Industries fortune, has raised the issue of Thurmond's age and his increasing dependence on his aides.
